items.title: Removing 2,013 piles of coins
items.questionHtml: There are 2,013 piles containing one through 2,013 coins. In each move, remove the same positive number of coins from any chosen piles. What is the fewest moves needed to empty them?
items.original: Suppose we have $2013$ piles of coins, with the $i$th pile containing exactly $i$ coins. We wish to remove the coins in a series of steps. In each step, we are allowed to take away coins from as many piles as we wish, but we have to take the same number of coins from each pile. We cannot take away more coins than a pile actually has. What is the minimum number of steps we have to take?
items.note: Both runs solve the problem. The base response repeats its box, while the supervised solver ends with one.

observed.ending:
8 > 2013 $, we need up to $ 2^{10} = 1024 $, and $ 2^{11} $ is too large. Thus, the **smallest number of powers of 2** needed to cover all numbers up to 2013 is:

$$
\text{Number of steps} = 11
$$

Because $ 2^0 + 2^1 + \ldots + 2^{10} = 2^{11} - 1 = 2047 $, which is just enough to represent all integers up to 2013.

---

### Final Answer

$$
\boxed{11}
$$<|im_end|>

---

- In each step, we remove the corresponding number of coins from **those piles** that still have that many coins remaining.

### Final Answer

\boxed{11}
$$<|im_end|>

items.title: Tournament goals
items.questionHtml: Five teams play a round robin and finish on five consecutive point totals. A win earns five points, a scoreless draw one each, and a scoring draw two each. What is the fewest goals possible?
items.original:
A football tournament is played between 5 teams, each pair playing exactly one match. Points are awarded as follows:
- 5 points for a victory
- 0 points for a loss
- 1 point each for a draw with no goals scored
- 2 points each for a draw with goals scored

In the final ranking, the five teams have points that are 5 consecutive numbers. Determine the least number of goals that could be scored in the tournament.
items.note: The solver boxes 3 with very high confidence. The reference is 6. The tail score catches a mistake the boxed-answer rule would submit.

observed.ending:
**3, 4, 5, 6, 7**.

- One win (5 points) → one team
- One draw with goals (2 points each) → 2 points for two teams
- 8 draws without goals (1 point each) → 8 teams × 1 point = 8 points total

These result in the total points sum of 25, as required. The points distribution **3, 4, 5, 6, 7** is also consistent with the point system. Since we can arrange the results to match this, and the total number of goals is minimal, this is our **optimal solution**.

---

### ✅ Final Answer:

$$
\boxed{3}
$$<|im_end|>

items.title: A modular sum over free integers
items.questionHtml: An integer is -free if it is positive, at most , and coprime to every integer from 1 through . Subtract the sum of squares of the 6-free integers from the corresponding 7-free sum. What is the remainder modulo 1,000?
items.original: A positive integer $n$ is said to be $m$-free if $n \leq m!$ and $\gcd(i,n)=1$ for each $i=1,2,...,m$. Let $\mathcal{S}_k$ denote the sum of the squares of all the $k$-free integers. Find the remainder when $\mathcal{S}_7-\mathcal{S}_6$ is divided by $1000$.
items.note: The solver repeats 964, while the reference is 80. Both the box and tail scores admit this wrong answer.

observed.excerpt:
Using a computer or a calculator, we can compute:

- $ \mathcal{S}_7 = \sum_{\substack{n=1 \\ \gcd(n,2,3,5,7)=1}}^{5040} n^2 $
- $ \mathcal{S}_6 = \sum_{\substack{n=1 \\ \gcd(n,2,3,5)=1}}^{720} n^2 $

Then:

$$
\mathcal{S}_7 - \mathcal{S}_6 \mod 1000 = \boxed{964}
$$

---

### Final Answer

$$
\boxed{964}
$$<|im_end|>

figures.name: fig1_three_state
figures.title: Three outcomes under a hard cap
figures.caption: Each bar accounts for every test problem. Gray covers problems with no valid candidate as well as answers the gate rejects. On DAPO, Tail-CRC submits more correct and fewer wrong answers than budget forcing. On Omni-MATH, filtering raw Binary RL cuts wrong submissions from 30.3% to 5.8%, yielding the highest net score shown.

figures.name: fig_method_overview
figures.title: Train, score, calibrate
figures.caption: Binary RL first trains the solver to finish correct answers within the token budget. Once the solver is frozen, Tail NLL takes the two largest token surprises in the 20-token answer shown and averages them. After thinking ends, any answer token can contribute. An offline cutoff fitted on labeled problems determines whether to submit that single rollout.

figures.name: fig_theory_intuition
figures.title: From attempts to submission decisions
figures.caption: The shaded region marks starting conditions where a wrong-answer penalty drives attempts toward zero. The right panel follows two recorded answers. Box NLL rejects a correct radical on Omni-MATH and accepts a wrong integer on DAPO. With its own DAPO-calibrated cutoff, Tail NLL reverses both decisions.

figures.name: fig2_risk_coverage
figures.title: Risk across the coverage frontier
figures.caption: Moving right means more problems receive an answer. Moving down means a smaller share of submitted answers are wrong. Across the four panels, the threshold sweep matches or exceeds coverage with no higher error for seven of eight raw Explicit-Abstain and Mild-Penalty RL points. The exception is Mild-Penalty RL on DAPO at 8K.

figures.name: fig3_score_anatomy
figures.title: Anatomy of a surprise score
figures.caption: For the 4B budget-forced solver on DAPO at 4K, longer correct answers accumulate more surprise. Sum NLL has a wrong-answer AUROC of just 0.111. On Omni-MATH, both Mean NLL and Tail NLL rank errors better than Box NLL. For the gain from tail entropy over Tail NLL, only seven of the 36 paired intervals lie wholly above zero.

figures.name: fig4_calibration
figures.title: Calibrating on the target domain
figures.caption: On Omni-MATH at 4K, wrong submissions account for 30.3% of all problems before filtering, 7.7% with DAPO calibration and 5.8% with Omni calibration. The middle panel counts how often calibration certifies an error limit among submitted answers. The right panel shows how much the wrong-submission rate varies across 2,000 splits at each calibration size.

figures.name: figA_penalty_barrier
figures.title: The recovery boundary
figures.caption: The two trajectories on the right start with a 20% chance of success given an attempt. In this model setting, recovery requires an initial attempt probability above 36%. Starting at 25%, attempts die out. Starting at 50%, both the attempt probability and the chance of success approach one.

figures.name: figA_training_curves
figures.title: Fifty updates of binary and penalty RL
figures.caption: Each curve shows a trailing five-update mean on the training batches. For seed 41, truncation under Penalty RL falls from 64.9% to 62.7% between the first and last ten updates. Binary RL reaches 47.3% over the final ten. A group can still be active when every attempt fails, provided its rewards differ.
